query: For W–Cu metal-matrix composites used in heat-dissipation and fusion-reactor joint applications, what single intervention could increase thermal conductivity while retaining mechanical durability and irradiation resistance? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the outcome relative to an otherwise comparable W–Cu composite, defines the application conditions under which it should hold, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a controlled, thin graphene interphase at the tungsten–copper boundary improves interfacial thermal transport and thus increases overall thermal conductivity while retaining the mechanical and irradiation performance of the composite.
generation.material_initial_state: A conventional W–Cu composite with direct metal–metal interfaces, where heat transport is partly limited by interfacial thermal resistance.
generation.intervention: Deposit a uniform, nanometer-scale graphene coating on tungsten particles prior to copper infiltration during composite fabrication.
generation.conditions: Under application conditions typical for high-heat dissipation and fusion-reactor joints, including moderate thermal cycling and prescribed levels of neutron irradiation.
generation.structural_mediator: A thin graphene interphase situated at the tungsten–copper interfaces.
generation.mechanism: Graphene’s exceptionally high in-plane thermal conductivity can bridge the tungsten and copper phases, reducing interfacial phonon scattering and thermal resistance. Its robust chemical and structural nature supports mechanical stress distribution and offers resistance to radiation-induced damage, thereby preserving overall composite durability.
generation.predicted_outcome: An increase in effective thermal conductivity relative to standard W–Cu composites, while maintaining comparable mechanical durability and irradiation resistance.
generation.baseline: Standard W–Cu composites fabricated without any interfacial graphene modification.
generation.boundary: The benefit is expected only if the graphene layer remains uniform and well-bonded; if the coating is too thick or not continuous, it may introduce defects or weaken the interface. Extreme irradiation doses beyond typical operational conditions might compromise the graphene layer, an uncertainty that needs further exploration.
generation.uncertainty: The long-term stability of the graphene interphase under severe irradiation and very high-temperature cycling remains uncertain, as does its behavior when scaling up production.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of W–Cu composite samples: one set with tungsten particles pre-coated with a nanometer-scale graphene layer via chemical vapor deposition, and another standard set without the coating. Subject both sets to identical thermal cycling and neutron irradiation tests. Measure and compare their thermal conductivity, mechanical durability (stress/strain behavior), and microstructural integrity.
measurements: Mechanical strength and toughness (via tensile or compression tests)
Irradiation damage (using transmission electron microscopy and other defect characterization techniques)
Graphene integrity (using Raman spectroscopy and scanning electron microscopy)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the graphene-coated composites do not show a statistically significant increase in bulk thermal conductivity over the baseline while maintaining equivalent mechanical and irradiation-resistant properties, then the hypothesis will be falsified.
